title: Executable eval case
description: AUTHORING.md §9. The `evals/<skill-id>/<case-id>/case.yaml` that the host's eval runner loads, as against the `tests[]` entry in skill.yaml that declares it. This schema says a case is **well-formed**. It does not say a case is covered, or tested, or that it passes: nothing in this package executes a case, and that is by design -- `adapters/runner-contract/CONTRACT.md` §1 puts execution, isolation and credentials with the runner, and the plan hands the running of these files to `claude plugin eval` on the host. Before this existed a `case.yaml` reduced to a single `tags:` line validated exactly as the full case beside it did, and an empty file was a valid case that satisfied `evals.declaration-without-case` and counted toward the three-case floor. That is what this closes, and it is all of what it closes. A case is configuration, not a durable run artifact, so it carries no envelope and is absent from common.schema.json#/$defs/schema_id.

schema_version.description: The loader's case format, not this package's version -- AUTHORING.md §8 keeps the two independent. Pinned to the one format this schema was written against, so a host that starts emitting a newer one is a deliberate edit here rather than a silent divergence between what the runner accepts and what this file describes.

name.description: The case's own name, which is not the directory name: the directory equals the `tests[].id` that declares it and is the join `ak validate` checks, while this reads as a sentence about the behavior.

tags.description: Case kind and release-scenario claims. Deliberately unconstrained beyond shape: which kinds a skill must carry is `REQUIRED_CASE_KINDS` in src/validation/evals.ts, and which `scenario-NN` values name a real scenario is `evals.scenario-tag-out-of-range` in the same file. Both are checks with messages that explain themselves, and an enum here would be a second, mute copy of them that could disagree.

execution.description: What the runner is asked to do. Closed on the three members AUTHORING.md §9 documents: a key the loader accepts and this does not is a schema edit, which is the direction that gets noticed.

prompt.description: The prompt the case runs. Required, and non-empty, because a case whose prompt is absent is the stub this schema exists to refuse.

max_turns.description: A cap the runner enforces. An integer count with no currency and no tier, like every other limit in this package.

allowed_tools.description: The tools the run may use. Not enumerated here: the set is the host's, and a case that needs a tool this package has never heard of is the host's business rather than a defect in the case.

graders.description: How the run is scored. At least one, because a case that grades nothing cannot fail and is therefore not a case.

items.description: Open, not closed, and the reason is a gap rather than a preference. AUTHORING.md §9 lists five grader types and documents the fields of three: `tool` for `tool_used`, `pattern` for `regex`, `expected_outcome` for `llm`. What `file_exists` and `tool_order` take is written down nowhere in this repository, and no case uses either, so closing this object would refuse those two types on a guess at their field names -- authoring a shape into the schema that no run has produced. The three that are documented are required below; the two that are not are left alone, which is visible here rather than silent.

type.description: The five types AUTHORING.md §9 lists. §9 also asks for a deterministic grader over `llm` wherever the pass criterion is observable, which is a preference a schema cannot hold.

allOf.description: An `llm` grader is its `expected_outcome` -- §9 asks for one 'that a reader could score by hand', and without it there is nothing for a judge to read.

A `tool_used` grader that names no tool asserts nothing about any tool. It is the eval-case form of a locator that matches no instance: it cannot fail, so it cannot grade, and nothing in this package would ever have said so because nothing here runs it. Inferred from §9's worked example, which carries `tool: Skill`, rather than measured against the loader, for the reason this object is open.
Same shape for the pattern a `regex` grader matches.
